newsitem.title: BELGIUM: No respite seen for Belgian T-bill yields.
newsitem.headline: No respite seen for Belgian T-bill yields.

text.p: Belgian Treasury bill yields edged up again on Tuesday and dealers predicted little respite unless money market rates ease.
"If the short end (of the money market) does not come down by 10 or 15 basis points then I think the long end (of the T-bill yield curve) will go higher," one trader said.

The trader said the level of money market rates meant funding new positions was impossible while funding older ones was expensive. "On a daily basis, everyone is losing money at the moment and at a given time it could become dangerous if people started to close their positions," he said.

Three month certificates were sold at an average yield of 3.42 percent on Tuesday, up from 3.39 percent last week. Six month certificates were also sold at 3.42 percent, up from 3.34 percent and 12-month paper was at 3.45 percent, up from 3.36.

Treasury bill yields have been rising steadily since they hit 35-year lows on January 21 because of a domestic political scandal that hit the Belgian franc, forcing the central bank to drain liquidity from the money market to attract money.
The money market yield curve remained inverted on Tuesday, with one-week repos at 3.50/55 basis points and 12 month repos at 3.46/51.

One trader said Treasury bills were hit by light selling early on Tuesday as investors played the difference in yields on repos. But while there was a net add of T-bills on Tuesday, with 41 billion francs sold against 26 billion maturing, dealers and analysts did not expect authorities to react to halt the slide.

They noted that T-bill yields were still below the average 4.10 percent rate the government took as its starting point for the 1997 budget, which is currently being reviewed, and that long-term interest rates were still the most significant factor influencing the cost of servicing Belgium's huge debt.
